svg.aria-label: How a sequence of Windows account and group-management events reveals an attacker creating a hidden admin backdoor, each step marked with its Event ID.
svg.title: Account and group events as a backdoor chain — reading persistence in the Security log
svg.text: A BACKDOOR ADMIN, WRITTEN IN FOUR SECURITY EVENTS
User account CREATED
A new local or domain account
appears — "svc-backup" or similar
innocuous-sounding name.
Added to a PRIVILEGED group
4732 = added to a local group
(Administrators); 4728 = added
to a global group (Domain Admins).
Special privileges at logon
The new account logs on and is
granted admin-equivalent rights —
confirming it now has real power.
The story, read as one
Alone, each event is routine IT.
In SEQUENCE, minutes apart, from
one actor: a fresh admin backdoor
for persistence + privilege.
WHY THE SEQUENCE MATTERS MORE THAN ANY SINGLE EVENT
Account creation (4720) and group changes (4728/4732) happen legitimately every day, so no ONE of them is an alert.
The signal is the CORRELATION: create → elevate → use, by the same actor, in a tight window, especially outside change-control hours.
THE HIGH-VALUE ACCOUNT EVENTS TO KNOW
4720 created · 4722 enabled · 4725 disabled · 4726 deleted · 4738 changed · 4728/4732/4756 added to (global/local/universal) group · 4672 special privileges
Watch especially for additions to Administrators, Domain Admins, and Enterprise Admins — the groups that grant the keys to the kingdom.
